mainTopic: How far a נדר of 'my loaf is forbidden to you' reaches, compared with הקדש: payment for מעילה on an ownerless loaf, and whether a forbidden loaf stays forbidden after it is given as a gift
overview: The amud opens with רבא ruling on someone who declares an ownerless loaf הקדש and then takes it. If he takes it to eat, he pays for מעילה on the whole loaf. If he takes it to leave to his sons, he pays only for the small goodwill benefit (טובת הנאה). Next, רב חייא בר אבין asks רבא about a נדר of 'my loaf is forbidden to you'. If the owner later gives that loaf to the person as a gift, is it still forbidden? רבא answers that it obviously stays forbidden. The words 'to you' make it like הקדש for that person. רב חייא בר אבין then asks what the word 'my' leaves out, and suggests a stolen loaf. רבא answers no: 'my' leaves out a case where the owner had already invited him to eat from the loaf before making the נדר.

steps.title: Using an ownerless loaf that was declared consecrated
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if someone declares an ownerless loaf הקדש and then takes it to eat, he pays for מעילה on its full value. If he takes it to leave to his sons, he pays only for the small benefit he got.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A loaf of ownerless bread was in front of a person, and he said, 'This loaf is consecrated.' If he took it to eat it, he committed מעילה, and he pays based on the whole loaf. If he took it to leave to his sons as an inheritance, he committed מעילה, but he pays only for the 'goodwill benefit' (טובת הנאה) he gets from it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new ruling about a person who declares an ownerless loaf הקדש and then takes it. How much he pays for מעילה depends on what he takes it for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating the loaf gives him the full benefit, so he pays for the whole loaf. Leaving it to his sons gives him no direct benefit. He only gains the goodwill that comes from giving it to them, so he pays only for that smaller value.

keyTerms.meaning: Ownerless property that anyone may take
Property consecrated to the בית המקדש
Goodwill benefit: the small value of choosing who gets something
To pass it on as an inheritance

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think that leaving the loaf to his sons is not מעילה at all. It is still מעילה. The only difference is how much he pays.

phrases.english: Rava said:
There was before him a loaf of ownerless bread,
and he said: "This loaf is consecrated,"
if he took it in order to eat it —
he committed meilah according to its entire value.
If he took it to leave as an inheritance to his sons —
he committed meilah according to the goodwill benefit in it.
phrases.notes: He himself does not eat it. He only gains the thanks and goodwill of his sons, which is worth very little.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הָיְתָה לְפָנָיו כִּכָּר שֶׁל הֶפְקֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens this section with a new ruling by רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Taking a consecrated ownerless loaf to eat means paying for its full value. Taking it to leave to one's sons means paying only for the goodwill benefit.

steps.title: Does a forbidden loaf stay forbidden after it is given as a gift?
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אבין asks רבא about someone who said 'my loaf is forbidden to you' and later gave that person the loaf as a gift. Does the word 'my' limit the נדר to while the loaf is his? Or does 'to you' make it forbidden to that person forever, like הקדש?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אבין asked רבא: If someone said, 'My loaf is forbidden to you,' and then gave it to him as a gift, what is the law? Do we say he said 'my loaf,' so it is forbidden only while it is still his? Or perhaps he said 'to you,' meaning he made it like הקדש for that person, so it stays forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חייא בר אבין asks a real question. He is unsure which word of the נדר matters more, 'my' or 'to you.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: the word 'my' ties the ban to the owner's possession, so once he gives the loaf away it is no longer forbidden. Side two: the words 'to you' put the ban on the other person, as if the loaf were הקדש for him, so it stays forbidden no matter who owns it.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him (a real question, not an attack)
'My loaf is upon you': a נדר forbidding my loaf to you
Or perhaps (introduces the other side of a question)

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין מֵרָבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Chiyya bar Avin asked Rava:
"My loaf is upon you"
phrases.notes: This means 'my loaf is forbidden to you,' said as a נדר.

phrases.english: and then he gave it to him as a gift, what is the law?
Do we say he said to him "my loaf,"
so only when it is in his possession is it forbidden?
Or perhaps he said to him "upon you,"
meaning he made it like הקדש for him?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין מֵרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question. רבא's ruling in step 1 was about real הקדש. This question asks whether a נדר of 'my loaf is forbidden to you' works like הקדש.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a נדר of 'my loaf is forbidden to you' stay in force after the owner gives the loaf to that person as a gift?

steps.title: רבא: the loaf stays forbidden even after it is given as a gift
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that it is obvious the loaf stays forbidden, even after it is given as a gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: It is obvious that even though he gave it to him as a gift, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question. The loaf stays forbidden, and he says this is obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא takes the second side: the words 'to you' put the ban on the person, the same way הקדש works. Passing the loaf to him as a gift does not remove the ban.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the נדר stays attached to the loaf for that person even after ownership changes. A gift cannot be used to get around the נדר.

phrases.english: He said to him:
It is obvious that even though
he gave it to him as a gift, it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: פְּשִׁיטָא דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּיַהֲבַהּ לֵיהּ בְּמַתָּנָה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The loaf stays forbidden even after it is given as a gift.

steps.title: Then what does the word 'my' leave out?
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אבין pushes back. If the gift does not help, why did the person say 'my' loaf? He suggests it must leave out a case where the other person stole the loaf, and a gift would seem to be just like that.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, the words 'my loaf is upon you': what do they come to leave out? Don't they come to leave out a case where he stole it from him?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חייא בר אבין challenges רבא's answer. He asks what job the word 'my' is doing if it does not limit the נדר to the owner's possession.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His suggestion is that 'my' leaves out a case where the other person stole the loaf: there it would be allowed, since the loaf left the owner's hands. If so, a gift, where the loaf also leaves the owner's hands, should be allowed too.

keyTerms.meaning: To leave out what? (asking what case a word excludes)
Is it not? (leads into a suggested answer)

phrases.english: But "my loaf is upon you"
what does it come to leave out?
phrases.notes: He is asking why the word 'my' is there at all if a gift doesn't free the loaf.

phrases.aramaic: לָאו לְאַפּוֹקֵי דְּאִי גַּנְבַהּ מִינֵּיהּ מִיגְנָב?
phrases.english: Isn't it to leave out a case where he stole it from him?

steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that the loaf stays forbidden after it is given as a gift
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'my' must leave something out. If it leaves out a stolen loaf, where the loaf left the owner's hands, then a gift should be allowed too.

steps.title: The word 'my' leaves out a loaf he had already invited him to
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that 'my' does not leave out a stolen loaf. It leaves out a case where the owner had already invited the other person to eat from the loaf before making the נדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: No. It comes to leave out a case where he had invited him to eat from it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge by naming a different case that the word 'my' leaves out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner had already invited the person to eat from the loaf before the נדר, that share is no longer fully 'his,' so 'my loaf' does not cover it. This gives the word 'my' a job without allowing a loaf that was given as a gift.

keyTerms.meaning: To it (to eat from the loaf)

steps.whatToRemember: A נדר of 'my loaf is forbidden to you' works like הקדש: the loaf stays forbidden to that person even after it is given to him as a gift. The word 'my' only leaves out a loaf the owner had already invited him to eat from.

phrases.english: He said to him: No,
it comes to leave out a case where he had invited him to eat from it.
phrases.notes: He invited him before making the נדר, so the share he offered already belongs to the guest.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא, לְאַפּוֹקֵי דְּאִי אַזְמְנֵיהּ עֲלַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 4 and keeps רבא's ruling from step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a different case that the word excludes
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'my' leaves out a stolen loaf, so a loaf given as a gift should be allowed too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word 'my' leaves out a loaf the owner had invited him to eat from before the נדר. A loaf given as a gift stays forbidden.
